title: 2.1.40 Conditionals Checkpoint Quiz
description: Five multiple-choice questions on === vs ==, operator precedence, and tracing three conditional snippets. Checked instantly.
sourceRef: designed: capstone quiz, assignment code A2.1.2 per curriculum-plan §2.1 Assignments; questions draw on book 2.1 Problem Set 2.1.7-2.1.10 intent (=== vs ==, operator precedence, trace prediction)

questions.question: What is the difference between === and ==?
options: They are the same; === is just the newer spelling
=== compares value and type; == converts the types first, so it can call two different kinds of value equal
== compares value and type; === only compares value
=== is for numbers and == is for strings
questions.explanation: `"5" == 5` is true because == converts first; `"5" === 5` is false because the types differ. Use === so the comparison never surprises you.

questions.question: In `age >= 13 && age <= 19 || hasException`, which runs first?
options: || runs first, because it appears later
They run left to right, so it does not matter
&& runs first: it binds more tightly than ||
Whichever one you put parentheses around
questions.explanation: && binds tighter, so it groups as `(age >= 13 && age <= 19) || hasException`. Writing those parentheses in changes nothing about the result: it just stops the next reader having to remember the rule.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Cold and Warm, on two lines
questions.explanation: 45 is not below 32, but it is below 60, so the chain stops there and prints Cold. An if/else-if chain runs at most one branch: the first one that matches.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: 72 fails the first two tests and passes `score >= 70`, so grade becomes "C". A chained ternary is read exactly like an if/else-if chain: top to bottom, first match wins.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The left side is false, so || hands back the right side: the string "Sunday", which is truthy. It never compares day to "Sunday" at all. You have to write the comparison twice: `day === "Saturday" || day === "Sunday"`.
